Borrowed from Byzantine Greek οἰάκιον (oiákion), diminutive of Ancient Greek οἴαξ (oíax, “helm, tiller”).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἀνόφθαλμος (anóphthalmos, “without eye”).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ἀνόφθαλμος (anóphthalmos, “lacking eyes”), derived from Ancient Greek ὀφθαλμός (ophthalmós, “eye”).

parole.significato: regional name of several willow plants, especially Salix purpurea
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek βρύλλον (brúllon).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek κατεπάνω (katepánō, literally “[the one] placed at the top, or the topmost”).
From Byzantine Greek κουκουβάγια (koukoubágia).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek κοντάκιον (kontákion).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek δούκα (doúka, accusative of δούξ (doúx)), in turn borrowed from Latin ducem. See also the likewise borrowed doublets duce and doge.

From Byzantine Greek φᾰγ- (phăg-), perfective stem of ἔφᾰγον (éphăgon, “I ate, I devoured”), singular first-person aorist active indicative form (by suppletion) of ἐσθῐ́ω (esthĭ́ō, “to eat, devour, consume”).
Probably from Byzantine Greek φράκτη (phráktē, “hedge”).

parole.significato: galley (slender Mediterranean ship propelled primarily by oars and sails)
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek γάλεα (gálea), from γαλέη (galéē, “type of shellfish”), from Ancient Greek γαλεός (galeós, “shark”).
From Byzantine Greek κάγχαλος (kánkhalos). Compare Sicilian càncaru.
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek αἰγυπιός (aigupiós). Compare ghezzo < Αἰγύπτιος (Aigúptios). Documented in Italian since 1336–8.

Originally Tuscan, from Byzantine Greek μάραον (máraon, “sweet chestnut”), ultimately from Proto-Celtic *māros (“great”), referring to the size of the nut, related to Welsh mawr and Cimbrian môr, a borrowing.
Ultimately from Byzantine Greek μονόλογος (monólogos, “speaking alone”).
Variant of mostaccio; probably taken from Byzantine Greek μουστάκιον (moustákion, “moustache”) or influenced by the Neapolitan mustaccio. Compare the augmentative Sicilian mustacchiuni.

From Byzantine Greek παπαγᾶς (papagâs), from Arabic بَبَغَاء (babaḡāʔ), of onomatopoeic origin. Influenced by gallo (“rooster”). Cognate with German Papagei, Sicilian pappagaḍḍu-pappajaḍḍu, Spanish papagayo, and English popinjay.
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek πένταλφα (péntalpha), derived from Ancient Greek πέντε (pénte, “five”) + ἄλφα (álpha, “alpha”).

From earlier pedota, pedotta, from Byzantine Greek *πηδώτης (*pēdṓtēs, “helmsman”), from Ancient Greek πηδόν (pēdón, “oarblade, oar”). The pil- forms are probably influenced by pileggiare (“to sail, navigate”).

parole.significato: a type of revolving wind rose
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek πινάκι (pináki), diminutive of Ancient Greek πίναξ (pínax, “tablet”). Doublet of pinax.

parole.significato: a boat used for sponge fishing
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek σαγολαίϕεα (sagolaíphea), compound of σάγος (ságos) + λαίϕη (laíphē, “sail”).

parole.significato: shroud (rope or cable anchoring the mast)
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek ἐξάρτια (exártia), plural of ἐξάρτιον (exártion), from Ancient Greek ἐξαρτίζω (exartízō). Compare Spanish jarcia and Catalan xarxa.
From Byzantine Greek σμερίλιον (smerílion), diminutive of σμερί (smerí), from Ancient Greek σμύρις (smúris, “emery-powder”).
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek σταυροπήγιον (stauropḗgion), derived from Ancient Greek σταυρός (staurós, “cross”) + πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “I secure, I fasten”).

parole.significato: stigma (a ligature of the Greek letters sigma and tau: Ϛ / ϛ)
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek στίγμα (stígma), likely coined by analogy with σίγμα (sígma).

parole.significato: pan (for cooking; especially a frying pan)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Byzantine Greek τηγάνιν (tēgánin), from Koine Greek τηγάνιον (tēgánion). The /m/ might be due to influence of the suffix -ame.

parole.significato: a type of conical stone-roofed house in Apulia (especially in Alberobello)
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek τροῦλλος (troûllos), from Latin trulla.

Borrowed from Byzantine Greek ταρκάσιον (tarkásion), from Arabic تَرْكَاش (tarkāš), from Persian ترکش (tarkaš), earlier تیرکش (tirkaš), derived from تیر (tir, “arrow”) + کش (kaš, “container”); modified by influence of turco (“Turkish”).
Ultimately from Byzantine Greek ἀθίγγανος (athínganos, “untouchable”), perhaps via French tzigane.
Ultimately from Byzantine Greek βόωψ (bóōps), *βῶψ (*bôps), accusative βῶπα (bôpa). Compare Albanian vopë, Greek γόπα (gópa).
